The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).

Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

1. Mental Demand

   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

     message.

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8
